Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: The author has no conflicts of interest to disclose.
The study was not preregistered.
Simulation code, trained networks, and pilot data are available upon request.
The author acknowledges support by the state of Baden-Württemberg through bwHPC and the German Research Foundation (DFG) through grant INST 35/1597-1 FUGG.
Evidence accumulation models are among the most successful formal models in cognitive psychology.

The diffusion model (Ratcliff, 1978; Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008; Voss et al., 2013) assumes that a decision between two response alternatives is based on the noisy accumulation of evidence until one of two boundaries is reached.
text.formatted: The diffusion model <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Ratcliff, 1978;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Voss et al., 2013)</ref> assumes that a decision between two response alternatives is based on the noisy accumulation of evidence until one of two boundaries is reached.

text.text: The model predicts the joint distribution of choices and response times, and it has been applied to perception, memory, lexical decisions, individual differences, aging, and clinical questions (Ratcliff et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The model predicts the joint distribution of choices and response times, and it has been applied to perception, memory, lexical decisions, individual differences, aging, and clinical questions <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Ratcliff et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Its parameters are interpreted as measures of distinct cognitive processes: The drift rate v reflects the speed of information uptake, the boundary separation a reflects response caution, the starting point z reflects a priori bias, and the nondecision time t0 reflects the duration of encoding and motor processes (Voss et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Its parameters are interpreted as measures of distinct cognitive processes: The drift rate v reflects the speed of information uptake, the boundary separation a reflects response caution, the starting point z reflects a priori bias, and the nondecision time t0 reflects the duration of encoding and motor processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Voss et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The validity of this decomposition has been supported by experimental manipulations (Arnold et al., 2015; Lerche & Voss, 2018; Voss et al., 2004), and it was also confirmed by a large blinded collaborative inference study (Dutilh et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The validity of this decomposition has been supported by experimental manipulations <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Arnold et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Lerche & Voss, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Voss et al., 2004)</ref>, and it was also confirmed by a large blinded collaborative inference study <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Dutilh et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In addition to the four parameters of the basic diffusion model, an additional parameter (the diffusion coefficient s) describes the random variability of the accumulation process within a trial.
This parameter is typically not estimated as a free parameter, but fixed to a constant value.

The reason is the scaling property of the diffusion model: The likelihood only depends on the ratios of a, v, z with s, and thus the predicted RT distributions do not change when these parameters are multiplied by a constant value.

To identify the remaining parameters, s is fixed to a constant, at s = 0.1 in the tradition of Ratcliff (1978) and at s = 1 in most current software packages (Fengler et al., 2021; Fengler et al., 2026; Henrich et al., 2024; Voss et al., 2015).
text.formatted: To identify the remaining parameters, s is fixed to a constant, at s = 0.1 in the tradition of <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Ratcliff (1978)</ref> and at s = 1 in most current software packages <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Fengler et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Fengler et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Henrich et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Voss et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In the literature, s is therefore often described as an arbitrary scaling parameter without psychological meaning (Donkin et al., 2009; Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008).
text.formatted: In the literature, s is therefore often described as an arbitrary scaling parameter without psychological meaning <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Donkin et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: It can be argued, however, that this view is incomplete.
The diffusion coefficient has a clear psychological interpretation: It quantifies the amount of random variability in the accumulation of evidence, that is, cognitive noise.
Fixing s to a constant implicitly makes the assumption that cognitive noise is identical for all persons and all conditions.
As a consequence, drift and boundary are measured in units of the individual noise level.
When noise differs between persons or conditions, observed differences in drift or boundary separation become ambiguous.
A lower drift rate in one group may reflect less signal or more noise, and a smaller boundary separation may reflect less caution or more noise.
I argue that cognitive noise is a psychologically meaningful construct, and that its measurement can contribute to the understanding of cognitive processes.
In this article, two different evidence accumulation frameworks are presented that make it possible to separate signal strength and cognitive noise from behavioral data.
Both approaches replace the conventional scaling assumption by a substantive assumption about the way information enters the decision process.

The Bounded Drift approach assumes that the drift is a bounded function of stimulus information and that the maximum drift, which is reached for completely unambiguous stimuli, is the same for all persons.
The Random Walk approach assumes that evidence arrives in discrete samples of constant size at an individual rate.

In this model drift rate and noise are both consequences of the sampling process, and the unit of the evidence axis is anchored to a property of the information flow rather than to the noise, and the noise becomes a free parameter.
The article is organized as follows.
First, the diffusion process and its scaling property are described, and consequences of fixing the diffusion coefficient are discussed.
Then, I review previous attempts at identifying the diffusion coefficient and introduce the two new approaches, including their formal specification and the assumptions that provide identification.

Because the Random Walk Model has no tractable likelihood function in the form used here, the models were fit with amortized Bayesian inference using neural networks (Radev et al., 2022; Radev et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Because the Random Walk Model has no tractable likelihood function in the form used here, the models were fit with amortized Bayesian inference using neural networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Radev et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Radev et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Simulation studies on parameter recovery and calibration are presented, followed by an empirical pilot study in which both models were fitted to the same data from five younger and five older adults.
The paper closes with a discussion of cognitive noise as a construct and of the research program that is needed to validate its measurement.
The diffusion model describes the accumulation of evidence as a Wiener process with drift (Figure 1).

text.text: The state of the process X(t) starts at the starting point za, where z is the relative starting point in (0, 1) and a is the boundary separation, and it evolves according to the stochastic differential equation where v is the drift rate, s is the diffusion coefficient, and W(t) is a standard Wiener process.

The process terminates when it reaches the upper boundary a or the lower boundary 0, and the response time is the sum of the decision time (i.e., the duration of the decision process) and the nondecision time t0.
In its full form, the model includes across-trial variabilities of drift, starting point, and nondecision time (Ratcliff & Tuerlinckx, 2002).

text.text: In this process, the diffusion coefficient 𝑠 scales the random noise.
A simple way to understand the role of s is to look at a simulation of the process.

With the Euler method and a step size of Δt, the process is simulated as with, for example, Δt = 0.001 s. 1 In every time step, the process moves by a deterministic amount v•Δt and by a random amount with standard deviation 𝑠 • √𝛥𝑡.

text.text: For a time step of one second (Δt = 1 s), the standard deviation of the random increment equals s.
Thus, s is the expected random movement of the decision process in one second, and the drift rate v is the expected systematic movement in one second.
The Diffusion Model Note.
The decision process starts at the starting point z and drifts with mean rate v toward one of the boundaries (a or 0).

In reality, t₀ comprises processes happening before (encoding) and after (motor response execution) the decision process.
Two sample paths are shown, one terminating at the upper boundary (blue) and one at the lower boundary (red).
The distributions above and below the boundaries are the predicted response time distributions for the two responses.
The scale of the vertical axis (information units) is fixed by the diffusion coefficient s, the standard deviation of the random displacement of the process within one second.

text.text: Multiplying v, a, za, and s by a common positive constant leaves the predicted choice probabilities and response time distributions unchanged.
The model is therefore not identified unless one of these parameters is fixed.
By convention, the diffusion coefficient s is set to a constant value for this purpose (Donkin et al., 2009).
text.formatted: By convention, the diffusion coefficient s is set to a constant value for this purpose <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Donkin et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The remaining identified quantities are the signal-to-noise ratio v/s and the boundary-to-noise ratio a/s (the relative starting point z is unaffected by scaling).
This convention has a direct consequence for the meaning of the parameters.
With s fixed to 1, the estimated drift rate v is numerically identical to the ratio v/s, and the estimated boundary separation a is numerically identical to the ratio a/s.
In other words, the unit of the evidence axis is the amount of random movement that the process makes in one second.
This is called an information unit in this paper.

A drift rate of v = 1 means that the systematic movement of the process in one second equals the random movement; a boundary separation of a = 1 means that the amount of information that is required for a response equals the contribution of the noise in one second.
Drift rates and boundary separations are thus relative quantities, scaled by the noise of the person whose data are analyzed.
Using a constant diffusion coefficient amounts to the assumption that all persons and all conditions have the same amount of cognitive noise.
This assumption is rarely made explicit, and there is no empirical evidence that supports it.
On the contrary, there are theoretical reasons to expect that the amount of random variability in the accumulation process might differ between persons, states, and tasks.

The neural noise hypothesis of cognitive aging, for instance, attributes age-related cognitive decline to an increase in the randomness of neural information processing (Cremer & Zeef, 1987; Li et al., 2001), and states like fatigue, stress, or sleep deprivation plausibly affect the fidelity of neural signaling.
text.formatted: The neural noise hypothesis of cognitive aging, for instance, attributes age-related cognitive decline to an increase in the randomness of neural information processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Cremer & Zeef, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Li et al., 2001)</ref>, and states like fatigue, stress, or sleep deprivation plausibly affect the fidelity of neural signaling.

text.text: If such differences exist, they will be absorbed into the estimates of the other parameters in a standard diffusion model analysis.
Specifically, when a drift effect is observed, we know only that the signal-to-noise ratio differs between conditions or groups.
We do not know whether the signal, the noise, or both differ.

A decrease of drift in older adults in memory retrieval (Ratcliff et al., 2011; Spaniol et al., 2006; Theisen et al., 2021) or in general decision making in very high age (von Krause et al., 2022) is compatible with a reduced rate of information uptake, but it is equally compatible with an unchanged rate of information uptake and an increased level of noise.
text.formatted: A decrease of drift in older adults in memory retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Ratcliff et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Spaniol et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Theisen et al., 2021)</ref> or in general decision making in very high age (von Krause et al., 2022) is compatible with a reduced rate of information uptake, but it is equally compatible with an unchanged rate of information uptake and an increased level of noise.

text.text: The same ambiguity holds for the relationship between drift rate and intelligence (Lerche et al., 2020; Schubert et al., 2015): More intelligent persons may extract information faster, or they may process information with less noise.
Likewise, when a boundary effect is observed, we know only that the boundaryto-noise ratio differs.
A smaller boundary separation can reflect a lower response criterion, but it can also reflect an increase of noise with an unchanged criterion.
A further consequence concerns the structure of individual differences.
If noise varies across persons, all estimated drift rates and boundary separations of a person carry a common factor 1/s.

This factor induces positive correlations between estimated drift rates and boundary separations that do not reflect a relation between information uptake and caution, and it attenuates relations between the parameters and external criteria.
Interindividual differences in noise may therefore blur effects on the other parameters.
Finally, the scaling convention hides a quantity that may be of substantive interest in its own right.

Within the model, noise is a determinant of accuracy and speed that is logically distinct from the quality of the stimulus information and from the amount of information required for a response, and it is a natural candidate for a mechanism that is affected by age, clinical conditions, and states such as intoxication or sleep loss.
Two strategies have been discussed for freeing the diffusion coefficient.
The first is to fix a different parameter instead of s, for example a = 1 or v = 1 (Donkin et al., 2009).

text.text: Donkin et al.
showed that the choice of the fixed parameter is immaterial for model fit, but that it changes the interpretation of parameter differences between conditions.
Fixing a or v, however, is only a reparameterization.
The resulting estimate of s is again a ratio, s/a or s/v, and the identification problem is relocated rather than solved.
No new information about the noise is extracted from the data.
The second strategy is to use external covariates.

Nunez et al. (2025) proposed diffusion models in which drift rate, boundary separation, or within-trial noise are linked to observed covariates such as single-trial electroencephalographic measures or to person-level variables.
If the linking assumption is correct, the covariate anchors the scale of the evidence axis and all three parameters become identifiable.
Nunez et al. demonstrated good parameter recovery in simulations, including some robustness to misspecification of the link.

The limitation of this strategy is practical: Covariates with a high and known validity for one specific model parameter are hard to obtain, and the identification rests entirely on the assumed link between the covariate and the parameter.
Any identification of s requires an additional assumption, because the behavioral data alone are invariant to the scaling.
The important question is which assumption makes it possible to extract independent information about noise, drift, and boundaries from the data, is psychologically plausible, and can be tested.
In this paper I propose two such assumptions.
Both anchor the unit of the evidence axis to a property of the information that enters the decision process.
The first anchors it to the maximum rate of information uptake; the second anchors it to the size of a single piece of information.
The Bounded Drift Approach
The drift rate in the diffusion model depends on the quality of the stimulus information.
In many tasks, stimulus information can be varied parametrically.

Examples are the proportion of white pixels in a black-and-white array (Ratcliff & Rouder, 1998; Ratcliff et al., 2003), the coherence of random-dot motion (Palmer et al., 2005), or the numerosity of displayed items (Ratcliff et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Examples are the proportion of white pixels in a black-and-white array <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Ratcliff & Rouder, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Ratcliff et al., 2003)</ref>, the coherence of random-dot motion <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Palmer et al., 2005)</ref>, or the numerosity of displayed items <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Ratcliff et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: For such tasks, the drift rate is a monotone function of the stimulus information, and this function must be bounded.

There is a maximum rate (𝐿) at which a person can accumulate evidence, and this maximum is reached when the stimulus is completely unambiguous, that is, when every piece of information points in the same direction.
The Bounded Drift approach assumes that this theoretical maximum is the same for every person.
Here I fix it to an arbitrary value of L = 1.
For a stimulus that contains only evidence for one response, there is no ambiguity to resolve, and the accumulation proceeds at the ceiling that the task permits.

Individual differences in the quality of information uptake are then expressed by the slope of the psychophysical function, that is, by how quickly the drift rate approaches its maximum as the stimulus information increases.

With L fixed, the unit of the evidence axis is the amount of evidence that an unambiguous stimulus delivers per second, and the diffusion coefficient s becomes a free parameter that quantifies the random variability in units of this maximum drift.
Importantly, fixing the maximum possible drift is not the same as fixing the actually observed drift.
The bounded drift approach still allows for interindividual differences in all observed drift rates, as persons may vary in how close they come to the assumed maximum.
For a highly perceptive person, the drift rate for a stimulus with 40% white and 60% black squares might be close to the maximum, whereas for a less perceptive person it is notably lower.

text.text: The identification of s can be understood as follows.
For each stimulus type, the data identify the ratios 𝑣(𝑥)/𝑠 and 𝑎/𝑠, as in the standard model.
Across the six stimulus types, the identified drift ratios trace the function 𝑡𝑎𝑛ℎ(𝑘(𝑥 -50 -𝑐)/2)/𝑠.
The asymptote of this function equals 𝐿/𝑠.
Hence, s is identified by the level at which the drift rate function saturates.
This argument also reveals the importance of the chosen levels of difficulty.
When task difficulty is too high even for the easiest stimulus types, k will be low, and little curvature information will be available, which makes it difficult to estimate the asymptote.
In this case, k and s trade off against each other and both are estimated with reduced precision.
On the other hand, when the task is too easy (even for the difficult stimulus type), k becomes very high and cannot be identified precisely.
The second approach to estimate cognitive noise rests on a different assumption.
Instead of anchoring the evidence axis to the maximum drift, it anchors the axis to the size of a single piece of information.
Historically, the diffusion model developed from discrete Random Walk Models of choice (Laming, 1968; Link & Heath, 1975; Stone, 1960).

text.text: In a random walk, evidence is accumulated in discrete steps, and the diffusion model is the limit of such a process when steps become infinitely small and infinitely frequent (see Ratcliff & Smith, 2004, for a comparison of discrete and continuous sequential sampling models).
text.formatted: In a random walk, evidence is accumulated in discrete steps, and the diffusion model is the limit of such a process when steps become infinitely small and infinitely frequent (see <ref type="bibr">Ratcliff & Smith, 2004</ref>, for a comparison of discrete and continuous sequential sampling models).

text.text: In the limit, the mean and the variance of the increments become independent parameters, which is the source of the scaling problem.
In a discrete random walk, in contrast, the mean and the variance of the increments are both determined by the step size and the step probabilities.
If the (mean) step size is fixed, drift and noise are no longer free to trade off against each other and thus can be estimated from data.
The Random Walk Model assumes that pieces of information with a constant expected value arrive at a rate of r samples per second.
Each sample is a noisy percept of the stimulus, and it moves the process up or down by one unit, plus some random variation.
The unit of the evidence axis is thus one average step, and the boundary separation a is measured in samples, that is, as the number of pieces of information that are required for a response.
The rate r takes over the role of the speed of information uptake, and the noise is determined by the variability of the steps.
This yields separate estimates for rate, threshold, and noise.

text.text: For estimation, the model was reparametrized as follows: Instead of the rate r, the time τ = a/r required to collect a samples was estimated.

This quantity is the expected decision time for a perfectly informative stimulus, and it is estimated more robustly than r itself, because a and r are strongly correlated in the posterior when the data constrain mainly their ratio.

To estimate both models in a way that is robust to contaminant responses, simulation-based inference is used here (Cranmer et al., 2020) with BayesFlow (Radev et al., 2022; Radev et al., 2023), a framework for amortized Bayesian inference with neural networks that has previously been applied to diffusion models (von Krause et al., 2022).

text.text: In this approach, a neural network is trained on data simulated from the model with parameters drawn from the prior.

After training, the network returns the full posterior distribution for any new data set within milliseconds, so that the computational cost is paid once and inference is amortized over all later applications.
Because both models are treated identically, the comparison between them is not confounded by differences in the estimation method.

text.text: The summary network was a Set Transformer, which is invariant to the order of trials and compresses a data set of arbitrary size to a vector of 32 learned summary statistics.
The inference network was a coupling flow with 24 layers, which transforms the summary statistics into samples from the approximate posterior.
To make the networks robust to the properties of real data, two forms of data augmentation were used during training.
First, for each training batch, a random number of trials between 260 and 320 was retained, so that the networks tolerate varying numbers of trials per participant.

text.text: Before applying the networks to empirical data, the networks are validated in two ways.
First, parameter recovery is assessed on a new set of 300 simulated participants that were not used during training.
For each simulated participant, posterior means and a central posterior interval of each parameter are computed and compared with the true values.
Recovery is summarized by the correlation between posterior means and true values.
Second, posterior distributions are assessed with simulation-based calibration (Talts et al., 2020).

text.text: If the posterior is correct, the rank of the true parameter value among the posterior draws is uniformly distributed.

The aim of the pilot study was to apply both models to the same empirical data and to examine whether the noise estimates of the two approaches converge.

Because the two approaches rest on different identifying assumptions, agreement between their estimates would be a first indication that the estimates reflect a property of the person rather than an artifact of a particular assumption.
In addition, the study included younger and older adults to explore whether the noise parameters are sensitive to age.
Given the small sample, this second aim is exploratory.

Five younger adults (age mean: 23.6; range: 23-24) and five older adults (age mean: 73.6; range: 71-76) were recruited through Prolific (Palan & Schitter, 2018) and received a fixed compensation of £5.50 for a session of 15 to 20 minutes.

text.text: The pilot study was not designed to test hypotheses about age differences.

Its purpose was to demonstrate that both models can be applied to empirical data, to examine whether the noise estimates of the two approaches converge, and to obtain information about plausible parameter ranges for the specification of prior distributions in future studies.
For these purposes, five participants per age group were considered sufficient.
In Germany, there is no general legal requirement for an ethics committee approval of behavioral studies with healthy adults.

Following the criteria of the German Research Foundation (DFG), approval is required when participants are exposed to considerable emotional or physical strain, are not fully informed about the purpose of the study, are patients, or undergo invasive or neurostimulation procedures.
None of these criteria applied to the present study, which consisted of a brief, anonymous online perceptual task.
The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines of the German Psychological Society (DGPs) and the Declaration of Helsinki.
All participants gave informed consent before participation.
The experiment was programmed in lab.js (Henninger et al., 2022) and run online in the participants' web browsers in full-screen mode.

text.text: After giving informed consent, participants reported their age, gender, and highest level of education, and indicated whether they could see the screen clearly (with glasses or contact lenses if necessary).
They could optionally note a known visual impairment.
On each trial, a square pattern of 100 × 100 small black and white squares was presented in the center of a mid-gray screen.
Participants decided whether black or white squares were in the majority by pressing the A key (more black) or the L key (more white).
Six stimulus types with 40, 44, 48, 52, 56, or 60% white squares were used (Figure 2A).
text.formatted: Six stimulus types with 40, 44, 48, 52, 56, or 60% white squares were used (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2A</ref>).

text.text: On every trial, a new pattern was generated by placing the exact number of white squares for the respective stimulus type at random positions.
The realized proportion matched the nominal level exactly, and only the spatial arrangement varied between trials.
Because the study was run online, the physical size of the stimuli depended on the participant's screen.
Throughout the task, the response labels "more black [A]" and "more white [L]" were shown in dark gray in the lower left and lower right corners of the display.
Each trial started with a fixation cross presented for 250 ms.
The stimulus followed and remained on screen until a response was given.
After the response, a blank gray screen (with the response labels) was shown for 750 ms before the next trial began.
Participants were instructed to respond as quickly as possible while keeping errors rare, and to decide spontaneously when they could not tell.
Each block was preceded by a countdown.
The session began with 30 practice trials, followed by five experimental blocks of 62 trials each.
In all blocks, the stimulus type on each trial was drawn at random with equal probability from the six types, so the number of trials per stimulus type varied slightly across blocks and participants.
No trial-by-trial feedback was given.
Between blocks, participants could take a selfpaced break and started the next block by pressing the space bar.
The first two trials of each experimental block served as warm-up trials and were excluded from the analysis, so that a maximum of 300 trials per participant entered the analysisfoot_1.

The estimates of boundary separation correlated at r = .85 across persons, and the estimates of mean absolute drift at r = .92.

These two quantities are the ones that both models identify in the same way as the standard diffusion model, and the high correlations show that the two networks extract the same information from the data.

The diffusion coefficient of the diffusion model is conventionally fixed and treated as a meaningless scaling constant.

I have argued that this convention hides a substantive assumption, namely that all persons and conditions share the same amount of cognitive noise, and that it renders the interpretation of drift and boundary effects ambiguous.
I proposed two approaches that identify the diffusion coefficient from behavioral data.

The Bounded Drift approach assumes that the drift rate is a bounded function of stimulus information with a common maximum for all persons; the Random Walk approach assumes that evidence arrives in discrete samples of constant size at an individual rate.
Both models were implemented with amortized Bayesian inference.
Simulations showed that the noise parameters can be recovered with calibrated posteriors, and in a pilot study the noise estimates of the two approaches converged across persons.

In the following, I discuss the interpretation of the noise parameter, the relation between the two approaches, the limitations of the present work, and the research program that is required to validate the measurement of cognitive noise.
Within the diffusion model, the diffusion coefficient quantifies the random variability of the evidence accumulation process within a trial.
This variability has several possible sources.

Part of it is external: The stimulus itself may provide inconsistent evidence from moment to moment, as is the case for dynamic random-dot displays, or the sampling of a static stimulus by eye movements and attention may yield variable evidence.

Part of it is internal: Neural representations of the evidence are noisy, and the transmission and integration of neural signals adds variability at every stage (Gold & Shadlen, 2007; Smith & Ratcliff, 2004). Ratcliff et al. (2018) have shown how internal and external sources of variability can be separated experimentally by manipulating the variability of the stimulus.

(2018)</ref> have shown how internal and external sources of variability can be separated experimentally by manipulating the variability of the stimulus.

text.text: In the present pilot study, the stimuli were static, so that the external source of within-trial variability was limited to the sampling of the pattern, and the estimated noise mainly reflects internal variability.
The Random Walk Model makes this decomposition more explicit.

It distinguishes the perceptual noise σ, which determines how reliably a single sample points in the correct direction, from the step noise η, which determines how much the evidence increment varies in size.
The effective diffusion coefficient of Equation 8 combines both sources with the sampling rate.

The two models therefore offer complementary descriptions: The Bounded Drift model treats noise as a single parameter that is scaled by the maximum drift, whereas the Random Walk Model decomposes it into components of the sampling process.
The question which decomposition is more useful is an empirical one that depends on which components show selective effects of experimental manipulations and consistent individual differences.
It is important to distinguish the within-trial noise discussed here from the across-trial variabilities of the full diffusion model (Ratcliff, 2013; Ratcliff & Tuerlinckx, 2002).
text.formatted: It is important to distinguish the within-trial noise discussed here from the across-trial variabilities of the full diffusion model <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Ratcliff, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Ratcliff & Tuerlinckx, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Across-trial variability of drift, sv, describes variation of the mean rate of evidence accumulation between trials and accounts for slow errors; within-trial noise s describes variation of the increments within a trial and accounts for the fact that errors occur at all.
The two quantities are conceptually distinct and, with the present approaches, both can be estimated in principle.

In the present implementation, I omitted the across-trial variabilities to keep the models simple, following the evidence that their inclusion often has limited impact on results in studies from individual differences research (Lerche & Voss, 2016).

text.text: Whether the identification of s remains robust when across-trial variabilities are included is a question for future simulation work.
The two approaches rest on different and mutually independent assumptions.
The Bounded Drift approach assumes that the maximum drift rate is the same for all persons.
Obviously, the present data does not make it possible to test if this assumption is correct.

If a person's maximum rate of information uptake is lower than that of other persons, for example because of slower sensory encoding, the Bounded Drift model will absorb this difference into a higher noise estimate or a lower sensitivity.
The Random Walk approach assumes that every sample contributes a constant average amount of evidence.

Again, this assumption could be wrong; if the size of the evidence increment differs between persons, the Random Walk Model will absorb this difference into the sampling rate and the noise parameters.
Because the two assumptions concern different aspects of the process, errors in one assumption are not expected to produce the same distortions as errors in the other.
The convergence of the noise estimates in the pilot study (r = .74) is therefore informative: If either assumption were grossly wrong, the noise estimates of the two models should diverge.
The comparison also revealed systematic differences.
The Random Walk Model yielded lower boundary separations in noise units and slightly higher noise estimates than the Bounded Drift model.
These differences do not indicate disagreement between the models but follow from the way noise is defined.
In the Random Walk Model, noise depends on the stimulus through the term 1 -𝑚 2 in Equation 8, so that noise is higher for ambiguous stimuli than for easy stimuli.
For the comparison, I used the noise at m = 0, which is the maximum of this function.
The Bounded Drift model assumes a constant noise across stimulus types, so its estimate corresponds to an average over stimuli.
A reference point at maximum noise necessarily produces higher noise estimates and lower boundary separations in noise units.
This is a testable difference between the models.

The standard diffusion model and the Bounded Drift model predict that the shape of the response time distributions is invariant across stimulus types up to the change in drift, whereas the Random Walk Model predicts an additional change in the variability of accumulation.
Experiments with a wide range of stimulus information could discriminate between these predictions.
More generally, the two approaches can be viewed as members of a family of identification strategies that anchor the evidence scale to a property of the information flow.

Other anchors are conceivable, for example the assumption that the drift rate is a linear function of a physical stimulus property with a slope that is known from psychophysics, or the assumption that an experimental manipulation affects only the noise.
The approach of Nunez et al. (2025), which anchors the scale to a neural covariate, belongs to the same family.

text.text: The strength of a research program on cognitive noise lies in the convergence of estimates across such anchors rather than in any single assumption.
The simulation results show that the noise parameters can be recovered, but also that their posterior uncertainty is substantial with 300 trials.

For the Bounded Drift model, the posterior intervals of s were wide for large noise values, and the sensitivity k can be expected to trade off with s when the drift function did not saturate within the range of stimuli.
For the Random Walk Model, the two noise parameters σ and η were partly interchangeable.
These results point to the importance of the experimental design.
In the Bounded Drift model, s is identified by the asymptote of the drift function in noise units, so that stimuli close to the extremes of the information range are the most informative.
The present stimulus set, which ranged from 40 to 60% white squares, was chosen to keep accuracy below ceiling, but it may not be optimal for the identification of s.

In the Random Walk Model, σ is identified by the stimulus dependence of the step probability, so that intermediate stimuli are informative for σ, and η is identified by the shape of the response time distributions.
A systematic design optimization, in which the expected posterior precision of the noise parameters is computed for different stimulus sets and trial numbers, is the next step.
Amortized inference is well suited for this purpose, because the trained networks can evaluate thousands of candidate designs at negligible cost.
Next to the question of task difficulty and number of stimulus types, also the number of trials per person is important.

Plausibly, the required trial number for a stable estimate of s might be larger than the number required for the conventional parameters (Lerche & Voss, 2017), and studies on individual differences in cognitive noise should plan accordingly.
text.formatted: Plausibly, the required trial number for a stable estimate of s might be larger than the number required for the conventional parameters <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Lerche & Voss, 2017)</ref>, and studies on individual differences in cognitive noise should plan accordingly.

text.text: Amortized inference with neural networks has two properties that require attention.
First, the posteriors are only as good as the networks, and their validity must be established by simulation.
The calibration analyses showed well-calibrated posteriors for all parameters except the nondecision time, for which the posteriors were slightly biased relative to their very small width.
For the present purpose, which focuses on the noise parameters, the consequences are negligible, because t0 was recovered with correlations above .99.
Second, amortized inference assumes that the empirical data are generated by the model that was used for training.
If the data lie outside the range of the training simulations, the posteriors can be arbitrarily wrong without any indication in the posteriors themselves.

Methods for detecting such model misspecification in the summary space have been developed (Schmitt et al., 2024) and should be applied routinely, together with posterior predictive checks of the response time distributions.

text.text: The present work establishes that the diffusion coefficient can be identified and estimated.
It does not yet establish that the resulting estimates are valid measures of the intended cognitive constructs.

The validation of a new model parameter requires the same program that has been carried out for the conventional parameters of the diffusion model (Arnold et al., 2015; Lerche & Voss, 2019; Voss et al., 2004).

text.text: Different lines of research are important to ensure the validity of the approaches presented here.

First, design optimization, as discussed above, should establish which stimulus sets and trial numbers yield the most precise estimates of the noise parameters, and simulation studies should examine the robustness of the estimates against violations of the identifying assumptions and against the omission of across-trial variabilities.
Second, experimental validation should test the selective influence of manipulations on the noise parameters (Voss et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Second, experimental validation should test the selective influence of manipulations on the noise parameters <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Voss et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: A manipulation that is expected to affect cognitive noise, such as a concurrent attentional load, sleep restriction, or a pharmacological intervention, should change s but not the sensitivity k or the boundary separation.

Conversely, a manipulation of speed-accuracy instructions should affect the boundary separation but not s, and a degradation of the stimulus, for example by reducing contrast, should affect the sensitivity but not s.

The models also make the prediction that the maximum drift (in the Bounded Drift model) and the step size (in the Random Walk Model) are invariant across persons; experimental conditions that are designed to push the drift rate to its ceiling can test this prediction directly.
Third, individual differences research should establish the psychometric properties of the noise estimates.
The retest reliability of s and its consistency across tasks are the minimum requirements for interpreting it as a trait.
If cognitive noise is a general property of a person's information processing, estimates from different tasks should correlate; if it is task specific, the construct needs to be refined.

The relation of s to measures of intelligence and to the conventional drift rate is of particular interest, because it would show whether the association between drift and intelligence (Lerche et al., 2020; Schubert et al., 2015) reflects faster information uptake, lower noise, or both.

text.text: Fourth, substantive research can use the noise parameter to address questions that the standard model cannot answer.
Age differences are the most obvious example.

The neural noise hypothesis of cognitive aging (Cremer & Zeef, 1987; Li et al., 2001) and the processing speed theory (Salthouse, 1996) make different predictions about the locus of age effects, and the separation of signal and noise in the decision process offers a direct test.

The linear ballistic accumulator (Brown & Heathcote, 2008), for example, has no within-trial noise and anchors its scale by fixing the variability of the drift rates across trials.

text.text: The present approaches keep this feature and add a second constraint that anchors the scale of the evidence axis.
In this sense, the proposed models are more constrained than the standard diffusion model, not less, and their additional assumptions can be tested.
Cognitive noise is a quantity that evidence accumulation models have always contained but rarely measured.

I have presented two approaches that make the diffusion coefficient of the diffusion model identifiable from behavioral data, one based on a bounded psychophysical function with a common maximum drift and one based on a discrete random walk with samples of constant size.
Both were implemented with amortized Bayesian inference, both recovered the noise parameters in simulations, and both yielded converging noise estimates for the same empirical data.

I propose here that the amount of noise in the decision process should be treated as a measurable individual difference variable, and I have outlined the validation program that this proposal requires.
Six stimulus types with x = 40, 44, 48, 52, 56, and 60% white squares are used, and participants have to decide whether white or black squares are in the majority.

Because tanh(u/2) = 2Λ(u) -1, where Λ is the logistic function, Equation 3 is a logistic function of x rescaled to the interval [-L, L].

For a sensitive person (k = 0.90), the drift rate reaches its maximum already for stimuli with 56% white squares; for a less sensitive person (k = 0.15), even the most extreme stimuli produce drift rates far below the maximum.
